text: Our train entered under the huge vault of the Pest station. Bay Ganyo and I entered the buffet. Knowing that we would be delayed here for a whole hour, I settled myself quite calmly at a table and ordered breakfast and beer. Around me, a world—a swarm! And a fine world at that. The Magyars, you know, are not much to my heart, but, look, the Magyar women—I have nothing against them. Absorbed in the noise, I didn't notice when Bay Ganyo had vanished from the restaurant along with his saddlebags. Where is Bay Ganyo? His glass was empty. I looked around, searched with my eyes through the whole restaurant—he wasn't there. I went outside—onto the platform—well, Bay Ganyo here, Bay Ganyo there—nowhere! Strange business! I thought he had gone to the carriage to check if someone hadn't made off with his rug.

I went back to the restaurant again. There is still half an hour and more until the departure of the train. I am drinking my beer and gawking. Every five minutes, the porter strikes the bell and indifferently, with a lazy voice, announces the direction of the trains: “he-gesh-fe-ke-te-he-gi, kish-ke-resh, se-ge-din, uy-ve-dek.” A few English travelers are gawking at him, and he, apparently accustomed to the attention he attracts with his peculiar language, grins from ear to ear and, with an even louder and hoarser voice, continues: “uy-ve-dek, kish-ke-resh, he-gesh-fe-ke-te-he-gi”... – with a sharp emphasis on every syllable.

About ten minutes remained until the train's departure. I settled my bill, paid for Bay Ganyo’s beer as well, and went out onto the platform with the intention of looking for him. At that time, a train was slowly entering under the station's vault and, imagine, in one of the carriages of this train, hanging halfway out of the window, Bay Ganyo appeared—I could not hear him because of the locomotive's hissing. I understood what the matter was. When the train stopped, he jumped to the ground, ran over to me, and told me the following, with a large mixture of energetic curses which, with your permission, I will not repeat:
– Forget it, brother, I’ve worn myself out from running...
– What a run, Bay Ganyo?
– Oh, what a run! You were staring there in the inn, weren't you...
– Well? – I reply.

– Well? In the meantime, you see, the one by the door rang the bell, then I heard the engine whistle, I go out – I couldn't call you – I see, our train has started off. Gosh! My rug! So I dashed after it, running and sprinting – don't even ask! Finally, at one point, I see it slowed down, and I – hop! – and inside. Someone shouted something at me, startled – heke-meke – I, you know, don't take any nonsense, I glared back at him, showed him the rug, anyway, he turned out to be an understanding man. He even chuckled a bit. Who was to know that we would be going back again. Hungarian business!

I, a sinful man, laughed heartily at Bay Ganyo’s adventure. Poor fellow! The train was maneuvering to enter another track, and Bay Ganyo ran, poor soul, for three whole kilometers to chase it – for his little rug was inside!...
– And you, in your hurry, forgot to pay for your beer, Bay Ganyo.
– Big deal! They fleece us plenty – replied Bay Ganyo in a tone that brooked no objection.
– I paid for it.
– You had plenty of money – you paid for it. Come on, get on, get on quickly so we don't have to go running after the train again – said Bay Ganyo patronizingly.

We entered the carriage. Bay Ganyo crouched over his saddlebags with his back to me, took out half a wheel of kashkaval, cut himself a delicate little piece, cut also a huge slice of bread and began to smack his lips with a wonderful appetite, puffing out first one cheek, then the other with his mouthfuls and every now and then stretching his neck so as to be able to swallow the dry bread. Bay Ganyo finished his meal, belched once or twice, shook the crumbs into his palm, swallowed them too, muttered under his nose: “Eh, if only there were someone now to treat me to a little wine,” sat down opposite me, laughed good-naturedly and after looking at me touchingly for a whole minute, said:
– Your Honor, have you traveled, have you wandered around much of the world?
– I have traveled quite a bit, Bai Ganyo.

– Oh, and what a lot of the world I’ve tramped through! Tsk... tsk... tsk... Never mind Edirne, Constantinople, but in Wallachia! Can you believe it? This Giurgiu, Turnu Măgurele, Ploiești, Pitești, Brăila, Bucharest, Galați – wait, let me not lie to you, I don’t remember if I was in Galați or not – I’ve been through them all.

Our journey to Vienna passed monotonously. I offered Bay Ganyo one of my booklets to pass the time reading, but he politely declined my offer, because he had read enough in his day, and deemed it more practical to take a nap. Why should he stay awake for nothing; since he had paid for the railway anyway, he might as well get some sleep. And he fell asleep. He fell asleep and snored so loudly that you wouldn't need to hear the roar of an Atlas lion.

We arrived in Vienna and stopped at the traditional Hotel "London". The servants took my bag down from the carriage and wanted to take Bay Ganyo’s saddlebags as well, but whether out of delicacy, who knows, he did not give them to them:

– How are you going to give it to them, brother, this is rose oil – it’s no joke, a strong scent – he’ll reach in to pull out a vial – go chase him after that! I know them. Don’t you look at them being so  o i l y  (Bay Ganyo wanted to say  p o l i t e,  but that word is still new in our lexicon, it gets forgotten), don’t look at them fawning over you. Why are they fawning? Do you think they mean you well? Eins, zwei! Gut morgen, and they’re always looking to snatch something. If not – a tip! Why do I take care to slip out silently when leaving the hotel... Beggars! A kreuzer to this one, a kreuzer to that one – there’s no making a living!
Since the rose oil that Bay Ganyo was carrying was indeed a quite valuable item, I recommended that he hand it over to the cashier for safekeeping.

– At the counter? – he cried out in a tone that sounded like pity for my naivety. – You're a strange lot, you scholars! Why, how do you know what kind of people they are at the counter? He pockets your rose oil, turns the corner somewhere... Well, and then? What do you do? Forget it! Do you see this sash? – And Bay Ganyo lifted his wide waistcoat. – I'll stuff all the vials inside. It's a bit heavy, true, but it's safe.
And Bay Ganyo turned his back to me (“the world is large, all kinds of people, who knows what this kid is too”) and began to stuff the vials behind his sash. I invited him to have lunch.
– Where should we have lunch?
– Downstairs, in the restaurant.
– Thank you, I don't feel like eating! Your Grace, go ahead and have a bite. I will wait for you here.
I am certain that as soon as I left the room, Bay Ganyo opened the lids. The man has his own food, why would he spend his money on a hot meal – he won't die of hunger, after all!

I took Bai Ganyo to the office of a Bulgarian merchant and left him there, while I myself got on the tram and went to Schönbrunn. I climbed the arch, looked over Vienna and its surroundings, wandered the alleys and the zoo, gawked at the monkeys for a whole hour, and returned to the hotel towards evening. Bai Ganyo was in the room. He wanted to hide his activity, but he did not succeed, and I noticed that he was sewing a new pocket on the inside of his *anteriya*. An experienced man, he wore a small *anteriya* even in the summer under his French clothes: “In winter carry bread, in summer carry clothes,” as the old people say; and so does Bai Ganyo.
"I sat down to patch myself up a bit," he said embarrassedly.
– You’re sewing yourself some kind of pocket; you must have made a bit on the side from the rose oil – I remarked jokingly.

– Who, me? You're mistaken! Why would I need a pocket here? Pockets, there are plenty, if only there were money. There's no pocket, nothing, it's just that my garment had come unstitched a bit, so I put a little patch... Where were you? Out for a walk? You did well.
– Didn't you go, Bay Ganyo, to take a walk, to see Vienna?

– What is there to see in Vienna, a city like any other: people, houses, luxuries. And wherever you go, it’s always "Guten Morgen", they’re always asking for money. Why should we give our money to the Germans – we have people back home to eat it up...
